title: Modernize auth stack: migrate JWT/OAuth libs, standardize TLS provider, refactor SAML adapters
creator: Anika Shah
description:
Summary: Replace several unmaintained or vulnerable auth/crypto dependencies and introduce an SSL provider abstraction so Dedicated/Private builds can use BoringSSL while Hosted continues on hardened OpenSSL builds. This reduces our CVE exposure surface, fixes token parsing edge-cases across languages, and simplifies SAML adapter maintenance.

Why: Recent dependency scans flagged multiple moderately-severe findings in legacy JWT and SAML packages, and our current OpenSSL pin (1.1.x in some images) is out of sync with cloud distro updates. Several customer-facing incidents were traced to token validation differences between services (python/node/Go). We need a coordinated upgrade that is low-risk and fully tested across runtime modes (hosted, dedicated, private).

Scope:
- Upgrade server and client OpenSSL in hosted images to 3.1.x where compatible.
- Add a pluggable ssl_provider abstraction in the runtime so Dedicated and Private packages can opt into BoringSSL for deterministic behavior and reduced platform patching drift.
- Migrate Python auth services from legacy-pyjwt (unmaintained fork) to python-jose; update downstream token validators and key rotation utility.
- Migrate Node services from jsonwebtoken@8.x to jsonwebtoken@9.x and standardize on jose for verification in a subset of services.
- Replace saml2 library usage in the SSO gateway with maintained fork (saml2-maintained) and refactor adapter wrapper to canonicalize NameID formats and assertion timestamps.
- Regenerate and validate internal root CA bundles in build pipelines and add a CI job to verify certificate chains against both OpenSSL and BoringSSL builds.
- Add fuzz tests and negative-case integration tests for token parsing (malformed claims, missing exp/iat, unicode escalation cases).

Plan of Work:
1) Branch: platform/security/eng/ENG-23764. Create feature flags: auth_deps_v2, ssl_provider.
2) Upgrade libraries in isolated service branches, update internal auth utility lib (authn-core) with compatibility layer.
3) Run unit + integration tests; add new CI matrix entries for boringssl and openssl-3.1.
4) Canary deploy small surface area services (auth-service, sso-gateway) using canary knob canary.auth_deps_v2=true. Monitor error rates, latency, and token acceptance rate.
5) Rollout to non-customer-critical services, then to Dedicated/Private images as opt-in.
6) Finalize by flipping default for new builds and publish migration notes for customers using SSO/Custom OIDC.

Acceptance criteria:
- No increase in 5xx auth-related errors in canary for 48h.
- Token acceptance parity with legacy stack for our canonical test corpus (>= 99.9% exact match on verification outcome).
- CI matrix passes for both OpenSSL and BoringSSL builds.
- Security team sign-off on dependency SBOM and reproducer tests.

Rollbacks & Risk:
- If token validation regressions detected, revert feature flag and deploy hotfix to authn-core to handle legacy token patterns.
- Performance risk: BoringSSL builds measured in microbenchmarks; we will run throughput tests and keep OpenSSL path available.
- Operational risk: private deployments that opt into boringssl must be documented since rolling upgrades require coordination.
